summary: BFD packets are usually tiny, so BFD only shows that a path works for small packets. This RFC describes how to pad BFD packets so they are large, letting two systems check that the path can carry a payload of a particular size, not just that it is reachable.

eli5.summary: Checking that a tiny marble rolls through a pipe doesn't prove a big ball fits. This sends bigger test packets to see if the whole path can carry them.

questions: how to test path size with bfd
how to test path mtu with bfd
subtitle: Pad BFD packets with zeros so a BFD session also proves the path can carry packets of a chosen size.

tldr.problem: BFD packets are tiny, so a BFD session going Up shows only that a path works for small packets. Some applications also need the Path MTU between two systems to meet a minimum.
tldr.mechanism: A new BFD variable, bfd.PaddedPduSize, makes the sender pad the BFD transport payload with zero bytes up to that size. If the path cannot carry the bigger packets, they are lost and the session goes Down.
tldr.outcome: BFD sessions can now double as a continuous minimum-Path-MTU check, with YANG modules to configure it. It is a Proposed Standard and it does not obsolete or update any other RFC.

today: RFC 9764 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Plain BFD Cannot Test Packet Size
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is commonly used to verify connectivity between two systems. BFD packets are typically very small, so a working session says nothing about whether a bigger packet would get through.

Some applications require that the Path MTU between the two systems meets a minimum. When it drops below that threshold they may wish to treat the path as unusable.

For directly connected systems, the link MTU configuration is typically enough, and BFD Echo mode is sufficient to verify the Path MTU. With multihop BFD that guarantee does not hold. Multihop BFD is carried in a simple UDP packet, and the base BFD specification is silent on the length of the encapsulation carrying the BFD message. The UDP payload is usually exactly the size of the BFD message, but nothing requires that, so it may be larger.
sections.eli5: A tiny test packet slips through almost anywhere. This RFC notices that nothing stops us from sending a bigger one, and a bigger one is a better test.

sections.title: The Padded PDU Size Variable
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new BFD variable, bfd.PaddedPduSize. The BFD transport protocol payload size, in bytes, is increased to this value. The extra payload MUST be zero, and the receiver SHOULD NOT validate its contents.

The variable must not be smaller than 24 or 26 bytes, the BFD control packet sizes permitted by the BFD receive procedures. When IPv4 encapsulation is used, the Don't Fragment bit MUST be set. Together these mean a packet that is too big for the path is dropped instead of being fragmented, so BFD notices.

The mechanism applies to BFD in Asynchronous mode. The RFC says it proposes no change to the BFD protocol itself.
sections.eli5: You pick a size and the sender stuffs the packet with empty padding until it is that big. The padding is just filler, and the receiver does not need to look at it.

sections.title: Peers That Do Not Support Large Packets
sections.content:
Some implementations may not accept arbitrarily padded transport payloads. A receiver that cannot take large BFD packets, or that wrongly rejects them during validation, behaves exactly as if the packet had been discarded. The BFD state machine then acts as if no Control packets were arriving and follows the normal procedures for that.

The consequence is that if large BFD packets are enabled on a session already in the Up state and the remote system cannot receive the padded packets, the session goes Down.
sections.eli5: If the other side cannot handle the big envelopes, it acts like they never arrived, and the connection is declared broken.

sections.title: Choosing and Checking the Size
sections.content:
Only the Path MTU the application needs has to be exercised. The RFC gives an example where the desired Path MTU is 1512 bytes while the interface MTU is 9000 bytes, so the padded size may be much smaller than the link MTU.

If several BFD clients want to test the same endpoints with different sizes, implementations SHOULD select the largest bfd.PaddedPduSize among the configured sessions, like BFD picks the most aggressive timers for multiple sessions to one endpoint. Otherwise a session can be Up while some application's MTU needs are not met.

To test the Path MTU in both directions, the parameter must be configured on each side of the session. For example, verifying a 1512-byte MTU both ways needs 1512 on both sides. Without consistent configuration the mechanism may correctly find unidirectional connectivity at the tested MTU but not validate the bidirectional MTU. Interfaces that intentionally differ can be set appropriately per side.

Once a session is Up, it keeps validating the tested size. If the Path MTU falls below it, the session goes Down. If the Path MTU grows, the session is not affected, because the mechanism only ensures the minimally acceptable MTU can be used.
sections.eli5: You only need to test for the size you care about, not the biggest the road allows. Both ends should test, or you only learn about one direction.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Other Forms of BFD
sections.content:
Link aggregation groups and equal-cost multipath (ECMP) forwarding spread traffic across several links while hiding the details from higher layers. A member link may not forward properly, and BFD packets may only be sent along links that are up, so a BFD session can be Up while some traffic is dropped on some component links.

BFD on LAG interfaces (RFC 7130) covers one such scenario, but for multihop paths there is no general-purpose BFD mechanism to exercise all ECMP links. Some implementations use internal knowledge of the component links to test them, but because load balancing is implementation specific, this cannot be standardized. Misconfigured member MTUs can make the Path MTU inconsistent depending on how traffic is balanced, and large-packet BFD is subject to the same limits. The RFC says this applies to most, if not all, BFD techniques.

The mechanism can also be applied to other forms of BFD, including Seamless BFD (S-BFD, RFC 7880).
sections.eli5: If a road has many lanes and one has a pothole, your test car might happen to drive on a good lane. This trick cannot promise every lane is checked.

sections.title: The YANG Modules
sections.content:
The RFC defines the ietf-bfd-large YANG module, which augments the BFD YANG modules from RFC 9314 and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture. A feature named padding must be enabled to indicate an implementation supports large BFD packets.

The module adds an optional pdu-size leaf, of type padded-pdu-size, to single-hop, multihop, LAG and MPLS session types. The type is a uint16 in bytes with a range of 24 to 65535. If the configured size is smaller than the minimum packet of a session, the session's minimum is used, and by default no extra padding is added. The module also defines a grouping, bfd-large-common, that BFD clients can reuse to add the feature uniformly.
sections.eli5: This part is the settings form network tools use to turn the feature on and type in the packet size.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The document does not change the underlying security considerations of BFD or its encapsulations. On-path attackers who can selectively drop BFD packets, including large ones, can make BFD sessions go Down. The padding is set to zero so that uninitialized local data is not leaked.

The one writable YANG node, pdu-size, is sensitive: changing it on an Up session may take the session down if it cannot accommodate the packets. Operators should remember that several BFD clients may depend on one session. IANA registered the XML namespace and the ietf-bfd-large module name.
sections.eli5: Someone in the middle can throw away your packets and make the link look broken. The filler is all zeros so no secret scraps of memory are sent by accident.

items.text: Packets are treated as discarded; an Up session goes Down.

items.title: Both directions
items.text: Configure the size on each side of the session.
